lesson.title: Counting Molecules: Molecularity Versus Reaction Order
lesson.summary: Molecularity counts how many reactant particles come together in one elementary step, a purely mechanistic fact, which is easy to confuse with reaction order, an experimentally measured property of the overall reaction.
lesson.body:
Molecularity is a simple idea: it is the number of reactant particles that come together and react in a single elementary step. Because an elementary step is one specific molecular event, that number is always a small, exact whole number, and it comes directly from how many particles you can physically watch collide or fall apart in that step.

A unimolecular step involves exactly one reactant particle, which rearranges its own bonds or falls apart on its own, with no partner needed for the step itself. A bimolecular step involves exactly two reactant particles colliding, and it is by far the most common type of elementary step, since it only requires two particles to meet, which happens constantly in any gas or solution. A termolecular step would require three separate particles to collide simultaneously, in the right orientation, all at once; this is extremely rare, because the probability of three independent particles arriving at the same point in space at the same instant, correctly oriented, is far lower than the probability of just two particles meeting. Almost every real mechanism you will study is built entirely from unimolecular and bimolecular steps.

Look back at the NO2 and CO mechanism from the previous chapter:

Step 1: NO2 + NO2 -> NO3 + NO (two reactant particles colliding: bimolecular)
Step 2: NO3 + CO -> NO2 + CO2 (two reactant particles colliding: bimolecular)

Both steps here are bimolecular, since each one involves exactly two particles coming together. That also means that for each step individually, you can write its rate law straight from its molecularity: step 1's rate law is k1[NO2]^2, matching its molecularity of 2 (two NO2 molecules), and step 2's rate law would be k2[NO3][CO], also matching its molecularity of 2.

Now for the distinction that matters most in this whole unit: molecularity is not the same thing as reaction order, even though the two ideas look similar and are easy to mix up. Molecularity applies only to a single elementary step, is a physical count of colliding particles, and is always a small whole number: 1, 2, or (rarely) 3. Reaction order applies to the overall, experimentally measured rate law of a whole reaction, and it can be zero, a fraction, a negative number, or a whole number, and in general it does not have to match the stoichiometric coefficients of the overall balanced equation at all. The two ideas only coincide in one specific circumstance: when an overall reaction genuinely happens to be a single elementary step, with nothing else going on, then and only then does its reaction order equal its molecularity. For any reaction built from more than one step, which describes most real reactions, the overall order is set by the rate-determining step's molecularity, not by the stoichiometric coefficients of the overall equation, exactly as you saw in the reaction mechanisms chapter's NO2 plus CO example, where the overall equation's coefficients (1 and 1) do not match the experimentally relevant orders (2 and 0) at all. The next chapter shows how to pin down real reaction orders experimentally, without relying on any assumption about mechanism at all.
